So I'm not being a dick, but here's some side advice that has gotten me pretty far in my career (i.e. hundreds of thousand per year working in software engineering):

Labor is a commodity, it's bought and sold. You're selling your labor to the company for a price, and they're buying it for that price. It's your job to maximize your cost and minimize your work, and it's their job to minimize your cost and maximize your work. Don't ever get emotional or frustrated about a company doing this sort of thing as it's exactly what they're supposed to be doing. Ironically, you're the one in the wrong here as you haven't been adjusting the price of your labor over the last 5 years, and you can't be surprised that they are going to do everything they can to keep buying it at a discounted price when you want to increase it now. Every single day is a renegotiation of your employment, whether you or your employer realize it.

With that said, either one of two things is true. First, you may not like to hear this, but it's possible that you're not nearly worth as much as you think, which is why they don't want to pay you more. I'm not saying this is true, but you have to accept the possibility that the market value of your labor is not what you think it is. Whatever you decide to do, your strategy should first revolve around ensuring that you're correctly gauging what the fair market value for your labor actually is, and what extra value you add specifically for your company. Talk is cheap, the only thing that matters in this case is money, not time nor seniority. You have to show how much money you make for the company, how much you're underpaid, and that you're underpaid compared to your peers. If you make the same as your peers, and bring in the same amount of profit, then you probably aren't getting a raise whether you like it or not.

Second, presuming that your labor is actually worth more, then your only choice is to sell your labor for more money (or reduce the amount of work you do, e.g. don't do the pedo's job anymore). If the company refuses to do either, then sell it somewhere else. Either way though, you need to approach the negotiation with the understanding that this is 100% your fault because you let it happen, and being upset at them is only going to weaken your position (either when negotiating in person, or when writing your 'priorities' as above, which are currently 100% based on feelings). Remember, you don't intrinsically deserve anything, and they're not responsible to ensure you're paid fairly, nor that you have a work/life balance, good mental health, etc. It's your job to get those benefits as part of the cost of your labor, and if they don't want to pay your cost (or reduce your work) then it's your job to walk.

Sure you're planning on leaving, but what if you end up having to stay another year for some reason? Also, I know doing the "fuck you" thing is cathartic (trust me, I've been in similar situations so I completely understand), but honestly if you end up doing anything but fantasizing about it for fun you're probably going to end even more frustrated than you are now. My advice is to go about things in good faith with clear asks (e.g. the exact raise/title change you want) and justification (e.g. your peers get tipped, but you haven't been), and go from there. If you're polite and professional the worst they can do is say no, but they won't hold it against you. If you go about it in bad faith, they''ll probably say no out of spite and then also screw with you (it's human nature to resist someone telling you to do something, even if you wanted to do it in the first place!).

I know Trump is controversial in these parts, but he's made two good points about negotiation. Never go into a negotiation without leverage, and never go in without being 100% willing to walk away. If you have neither of those right this second (i.e. you're not ready to give your 2 weeks on the spot), I would just keep my head down and look for another job. Even if you switch jobs and end up having to quit pretty quickly because you move to the country, you'll be much better off. Always plan ahead, but don't let those plans prevent you from making the best decision right now as you never know what's going to happen tomorrow.

Human trafficking wasn't illegal until 2000, when the Trafficking Victims Protection Act was passed, which made it a federal crime.

Since 2007, more than 49,000 cases of human trafficking in the US have been reported to the National Human Trafficking Hotline, which receives an average of 150 calls per day.
